reflections.body: Okay so. Dev took 26 hours to reply to a text that just said 'this weekend?' and by hour 4 I had already run the full simulation: he's bored, he met someone at that climbing gym, this is the polite fade-out. By hour 12 I'd drafted a breezy 'no worries if not!' that was neither breezy nor no-worries. He replied 'sorry, on-call weekend from hell, yes please.' So. The bug was on my end. Logging it.

Debugging note to self: I treat a delayed reply like a stack trace. Something threw an exception, therefore something is broken, therefore find the fault line before it takes the whole thing down. But a slow text isn't an error. It's just a human being who has a job. I know this in the way you know a fact you don't believe.

Weekly call with Paati. She doesn't text, doesn't 'read receipt,' just picks up Sunday 8pm her time like she's picked up for thirty-one years. No auditioning. She asked what I ate and I nearly cried into the sambar. Cheating a little — this is the one relationship I've never had to earn, so of course it feels safe. The trick is the ones I do think I have to earn.

Group chat blew up at 1am over which one of us would survive a horror movie (consensus: me, because I'd have already left the house on day one). And it landed funny because — yeah. I leave first. I called it 'reading the room' for years. It's not reading. It's pre-committing to the exit so the door doesn't get to close on me first.

Here's the thing I noticed and it's making me itch: I'm not anxious when Dev and I fight. We haven't fought. I'm anxious because it's GOING WELL. He remembered I hate cilantro. He called just to say goodnight. And my whole nervous system read it as 'the higher you build the further it falls.' Closeness registers as threat. That's — that's a really inconvenient thing to find out about yourself on a Tuesday.

Named it out loud to Valentina and it came out embarrassingly clean: I'm scared of the good thing. Not the loss — the good. Because good is the setup. Payyi vekkanum-nnu nenaikkiren — like I have to keep a bag half-packed so I'm never the one caught surprised. I've been calling it low-maintenance. 'Oh I'm so easy, I need nothing.' Needing nothing isn't a virtue. It's me disappearing slowly so no one has to do the leaving. Ugh. Caught myself even mid-sentence trying to make that sound cute.

Worksheet on 'the test.' Turns out I do run tests. I go quiet to see if they chase. I under-reply to see if they notice. And when they don't chase perfectly, I file it as proof. It's the most rigged experiment in the world — I designed it to fail so I could be right that people leave. Green-lit my own conclusion before I ran the data. Bad science, Priya.

It happened. Dev got quiet for two days — genuinely busy, a launch — and I felt the old script load: withdraw, go cold, get the exit ready. My thumb was on 'hey I think we should slow down.' The pre-emptive dump. And I just... didn't send it. Sat there. Let the wanting-to-leave move through me without obeying it. It was awful. Kadavule it was so uncomfortable. But I stayed.

Not a triumph, just a note. The discomfort of staying hasn't gone away — I don't think it goes away yet. But I noticed it's a different kind of hard than leaving. Leaving hurt clean and fast, on my terms, done. Staying hurts slow and open-ended and out of my control. And I hate not being in control. Still here though. Bag's unpacked, or at least — I put a few things back in the drawer.

messages.body: Hi — signed up mostly because I spent a whole workday half-writing a breakup with someone who was just on-call. I'd like that to be less normal for me, if possible.
That's a very precise place to start, and I'm glad you're here. I noticed you called it a logistics problem and then laughed. We might come back to what the laugh is protecting. No rush.
Weird question. Is it a known bug that the anxiety gets LOUDER when things are good? Because that's not in the manual I was handed.

Not a bug — it's the system working exactly as it was built. If closeness once meant a loss was coming, your body learned to brace when things get warm. We can look at where it learned that. You don't have to defend the observation, it's a good one.
Update: had the urge to send the 'let's slow down' text and didn't. Feels less like a win and more like I willingly held my hand on a hot stove. Is that the assignment??

That's exactly it, and I don't want to oversell it because you'll get suspicious of me. You felt the exit-reflex and didn't obey it. The discomfort you're sitting in is the old alarm going off with no fire behind it. Staying while it rings — that's the whole practice. Well done, Priya.

notes.body: Intake. Software engineer, razor-sharp, debugs her own feelings in real time — which is a strength and also her best hiding place. Presents an abandonment pattern as a 'logistics problem' and laughs at it before I can. Watch the laugh; it arrives right where the tenderness would. She names abandonment, over-monitoring, and her group chat readily. Two things she cannot yet see: that she leaves first and calls it self-protection, and that her prized 'low-maintenance' is a slow disappearing act. Not naming those yet. Let her find them.

Major movement this month, entirely her own: she caught that the anxiety spikes when things are GOOD. First time she's named the fear of the good thing. Tamil started slipping in around it — 'payyi vekkanum,' keeping a bag packed — which for her is the tell that the feeling has outrun the engineering language. That's where the real material is. She also self-corrected 'low-maintenance' as disappearance mid-entry. The unaware-of list is becoming visible to her. Do not rush toward resolution; the wound is only just being seen.

She reached the edge of the pre-emptive-withdrawal reflex and did not act on it. Notably she refuses to frame it as a victory — 'hand on a hot stove' — which is honest and correct for where she is. The belief is now visible and articulated but NOT yet loosening; she's tolerating the discomfort of staying without yet trusting it will end well, and control-loss is the sharpest part. Keep the frame gentle and specific. Resource to lean on: the grandmother's weekly call — proof, already in her life, that some bonds don't have to be earned. She hasn't fully connected that this could be possible with Dev too. Let her get there.
